title: Kahana vs Teachable: The Cohort Needs a Shelf
excerpt: Teachable is course hosting, student enrollment, drip content, and course checkout, a strong home for running and selling a full course. Kahana is discovery + cohort discussion around teaching you already run elsewhere.

columns.label: Ebook
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily get and consume ebooks on the platform (free or paid) as a first-class product, open, buy, borrow, or read without hunting.

columns.label: Short-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily consume short-form video as a first-class surface (For You, Reels, Shorts).

columns.label: Long-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch creator / UGC long-form video (or specialty long video) as a core surface. Course lectures belong under Courses. Hollywood catalogs belong under Series/Films.

columns.label: Series/Films
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch series and films as an SVOD / catalog entertainment product.

columns.label: Courses
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily take or browse structured courses as a first-class product.

columns.label: Newsletters
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily read or subscribe to newsletters / creator writing as a first-class product.

columns.label: Audio
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily listen to music, podcasts, or audiobooks as a first-class product.

columns.label: Memberships
columns.definition: Yes if a creator or seller can accept payments from others and make money through the platform, checkout, fan subscriptions, tips, ads, shop, or creator funds. Not only a classic Patreon-style membership product.

columns.label: Community & Messaging
columns.definition: Yes if you can create or join a group, community, or club, including group chats, Groups, subreddits, community tabs, discussion boards, or community feeds. A one-off comment on a single video or listing is not the bar; a durable place for the group to talk is.

columns.label: Storefronts
columns.definition: Yes if the product gives a creator a custom storefront or site that can take the place of building their own website (bio page, creator site, branded shop). Not a shop tab on someone else’s multi-seller marketplace.

columns.label: Marketplaces
columns.definition: Yes if a typical person can search and shop a catalog of offerings from many sellers, courses, books, digital goods, etc. Storefront software (Shopify, WooCommerce) is not a marketplace unless shoppers browse many sellers there.

scaleFacts: Historically reported 80,000+ published courses and 7M+ students.
ARR reached USD 26M in 2020; continued growth since.

strengths.title: Beginner-friendly course creation
strengths.detail: Simple UI to upload videos, add quizzes, build landing pages, email students, and accept payments from one dashboard with little technical skill.

strengths.title: Strong onboarding and support
strengths.detail: Good documentation and support; popular with first-time course creators for ease of use.

strengths.title: Rich course features
strengths.detail: Quizzes, completion certificates, coupons, affiliates, and basic analytics built in.

strengths.title: Unlimited courses and students on paid plans
strengths.detail: Paid plans support multiple courses and unlimited students; Pro plan offers 0% transaction fees.

weaknesses.title: Cost-to-value concerns
weaknesses.detail: Can be more expensive than competitors with broader feature sets; higher tiers feel costly relative to functionality for many users.

weaknesses.title: Free plan limitations
weaknesses.detail: Free plan is weak for selling, Teachable branding, limited features, and significant transaction fees.

weaknesses.title: Feature gaps vs “all-in-one” claims
weaknesses.detail: Lacks robust email marketing, advanced automations, and deep site customization; creators often need external tools.

weaknesses.title: Pricing jumps and transaction fees
weaknesses.detail: Big jump from Basic to Pro (e.g. ~USD 39 to 119/month); Basic charges ~5% transaction fees and lacks affiliates.

content:
Kahana is a library of curated hubs, Explore, Clubs, and optional Stripe. Teachable is course hosting, student enrollment, drip content, and course checkout, a strong home for running and selling a full course. They overlap in places and diverge in others.

What each one is

Kahana is built around hubs people can open, Explore so strangers can find them, Aura as scarce daily recognition, and Clubs so discussion outlives a feed. Selling stays optional.

Teachable is a platform that enables creators to build and sell online courses and coaching services.

Why this comparison

This article puts Kahana and Teachable side by side. It covers what each supports as a first-class product job, key features, and a few research notes so you have a clearer picture of what they are, how they compare, and what you can actually do on each one. It is not a teardown, and it is not a switch-tomorrow pitch.
contentAfter:
What you can do on each

On Kahana you can publish a hub, list it on Explore, discuss it in a Club, grant Aura, and turn on a Stripe paywall when you are ready to charge.

On Teachable you can use Courses, Memberships, and Storefronts as first-class product jobs. You are running a full course engine: drip, quizzes, student progress, and checkout that already works.

Using Kahana with Teachable

You can use both. Teachable keeps doing what it already does well. Kahana is another place to package the work, get discovered, and grow an audience.

Keep the course engine on Teachable for drip, quizzes, and enrollment. Also list or link that teaching on Kahana so Explore, Clubs, and Aura can give it another place to be found. Teachable stays the LMS; Kahana is another surface for exposure.
